newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia boosts gas processing for local needs.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia boosts gas processing for local needs.

text.p: Saudi Arabia will spend $2.5 billion dollars on domestic gas-processing plants over the next six years to ensure that the kingdom keeps pace with surging power demand, foreign contractors in Riyadh said on Wednesday.

State oil giant Saudi Aramco, in its largest expansion of gas processing in more than a decade, has gone to the market for the construction of a $2 billion gas plant at the Hawiyah producing zone of the huge Ghawar oilfield, contractors said.
"They need to recover their gas needs for the next decade," a contractor said.

Hawiyah dwarfs Aramco's other gas plant projects which focus on expanding capacity at three existing processing plants to meet growing gas demand from domestic electricity utilities, industry, petrochemical firms and water desalination plants.

"Aramco has looked at the power demand profile over the next 10 years and realised that the expansions were not enough...Hawiyah should give the country a safety net," one Western contractor involved in the energy business said.

A project manager for Hawiyah, which will be able to process 1.44 billion cubic feet a day of gas, is expected to be selected in November or December. Tenders are expected to be invited for the main engineering, procurement and construction contract at the end of 1997 or early 1998, contractors said.
Under the $2 billion project, which would come onstream between 2002-2003, Hawiyah would be connected by pipeline to Riyadh's power stations.

Hawiyah is being supplemented by expansion work at the Uthmaniyyah, Berri and Shedgum gas facilities, the backbone of the country's master gas system (MGS) which handles around four billion cubic feet a day of gas for the Eastern province.
When work at the four facilities is completed, MGS capacity should be pushed close to 6.3 billion cubic feet a day.
Contracts to boost Uthmaniyyah were expected to be awarded in October, Berri early in 1997 and Shedgum in the middle of 1997, company sources involved in the bidding process said.

Electricity consumption in the Saudi five-year development plan to 2000 is forecast to grow at an average annual rate of 6.4 percent, led by strong growth in the Eastern and Central provinces, according to the Ministry of Planning.
To meet this demand new power stations are coming on stream to boost power generation capacity to over 25,000-megawatts (MW) in the year 2000 from the current 19,000 MW.
Gas is used for 67 percent of all power generation in the kingdom, Ministry of Industry and Electricity figures show.
